Phosphate Namaqualand Mine - Elandsfontein

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Namaqualand phosphate mine threatens fragile biosphere

Unique Selling Point:
The world famous Namaqualand fdaisies that draw thousands of tourists every year are under threat from phosphate mines in the area. How were the mining rights for the Elandsfontein phosphate mine granted without a proper EIA? Why has Helen Zille supported the mining of phosphate which could be used in military weapons by Denel?

Press Release:


Phosphate Mining and the Famous Flowers
Mining rights have been granted to the Elandsfontein mine, located on a private reserve bordering the West Coast National Park. Carte Blanche asks: Was a proper Environmental Impact Assessment done and could the looming shadow of phosphate mining spell disaster for the Langebaan lagoon and its fragile biosphere—including South Africa’s world famous West Coast flowers?


Script:


ELANDSFONTEIN MINE

V/O: This is the West Coast National Park, a nature reserve surrounding the Langebaan lagoon. This world-renowned wetland is a RAMSAR site of international importance for marine life, and every year thousands of tourists flock to see the spring wildflowers. But within a hundred metres of the Park, this pristine landscape now bears the mark of mining.

Claire link: This is the entrance to the Elandsfontein Phosphate Mine that is currently under construction, and very close to being operational. However it has caused a controversy because it’s located on a very sensitive bio-diverse area on the West Coast, and is the subject of a current High Court appeal.

Carika: If it gets passed and it doesn’t get opposed and if it doesn’t get stopped then that will set a precedent. Then it means that no other national park in SA is also safe.

V/O: Carika van Zyl now lives in the sleepy village of Aurora, where she owns the local bakery. She used to be Conservation Manager of the Cape West Coast Biosphere Reserve but when she started an online petition to stop the mine, it cost her her job.

Carika: I knew that Elandsfontein was part of a critical biodiversity area, and also knew there was an aquifer on it that was maintaining the Langebaan lagoon. So immediately I realized, based on the available data, that this is not a good idea.

V/O: The Elandsfontein aquifer is an extremely significant groundwater system that releases mineral rich fresh water into the Lagoon, and feeds the marshes at the southern end which support bird life and act as a fish nursery area.

Carika: It is the water heart, it is the pump within a 30km radius of the area. If we take the pump out, then everything that depends on it to live is going to be affected.

V/O: But the Elandsfontein mine is directly on top of the aquifer, because the phosphate deposit occurs within the sand particles of the aquifer. This means they have to dewater the aquifer to get to the phosphate
Michelle: All the water that we are taking out is going to be put back into the aquifer.

V/O: Elandsfontein’s Michelle Lawrence showed us around the mine, and explained their water model.

Michelle: What we are doing is simply bypassing the mining area. We are sinking a number of boreholes around the mining area, we are removing the water from the mining area so that it is safe to mine, and we are recharging the water downstream of the mining area.

Claire: What effect will that have on the area?

Michelle: The findings of the specialist reports are that it has very low potential impacts on the lagoon.

V/O: But can they say that for sure? Christo van Wyk is Chairman of the Saldanha Bay Water Quality Forum Trust.

Christo: Our total focus is long term monitoring, and monitoring if there is any impact from the mine on the lagoon.

Claire: So how long will it take the Trust to pick up a problem?

Christo: We are monitoring the marine environment and that is 15km away. So that will have a year, even 2 or 3 years of a lag before we will pick up anything.

Carika: The problem is we do not know to what extent it will get affected because there was no EIA done.

V/O: Elandsfontein withdrew their Environmental Impact Assessment application from the provincial Department when legislation changed. The new One Environmental System means the Department of Mineral Resources is now the competent authority that evaluates environmental applications.

James: Environmental legislation makes provision for Environmental Impact Assessments which investigate all environmental concerns. This differs from the processes and assessments that the DMR would follow.

Claire: Was a comprehensive EIA done by the mine?

Michelle: We‘ve spent over R25 million doing 3rd party specialist studies and consultant reviews, and we’ve engaged in public participation processes. So a full Environmental Impact Assessment was done and that was submitted to the Department of Mineral Resources.

V/O: Mineral Resources’ evaluated the 1500-page document. They found that Elandsfontein had not met all the relevant requirements; the mine might result in unacceptable impact on the Elandsfotnein Aquifer and the Langebaan Lagoon, and cause ecological degradation and damage to the environment. Granting the right would result in unacceptable pollution and the application was not supported.

But by the time this Record of Decision was issued on the 27th of November 2014, it was too late. The application had already been approved by the Western Cape Regional Manager, and signed off by the Director General the day before.

Jana: If that report was not before him when he signed the mining right on the 26th of November, he was not entitled in law to sign that mining right, because he could not have been satisfied of the environmental impact.

V/O: Environmental attorney Jana Miller represents Carika van Zyl and the West Coast Environmental Protection Association. They have launched a Review Application in the Cape High Court.

Claire: What are you hoping to achieve with this case?

Jana: Our best outcome would be that on review the court decides that the mining right was not granted lawfully, and that that decision is reviewed and set aside.

V/O: We showed the Record of Decision to Michelle Lawrence, who was shocked when she read it.

Michelle: I’m gutted! Um…

Claire: The DDG couldn’t have taken any of the issues into consideration when approving the License?

Michelle: That question is relating to the internal workings of the DMR, so I'm not in a position to speculate.

Claire: The billion rand question is: why did the Regional Manager sign approval for the mining license without waiting for the Record of Decision. This is where the DMR is based in Cape Town. We asked them for an interview but they declined, saying that they were preparing to file legal papers and didn’t want to compromise the process.

V/O: Elandsfontein is also extremely rich in fossils. The 500 000 year old hominid skull Saldanha Man, was discovered in the dune field just 5km from the mine. Heritage Western Cape had to force them to do a Heritage Impact Assessment.

Penny: We issued in fact 3 stop works orders in all on the mine. They did not comply and we were forced to go to court. We served them with interdict papers, and eventually settled basically on the morning of the hearing of the interdict.

V/O: Attorney Penny Meyer acted for Heritage Western Cape.

Penny: In terms of the settlement agreement they had to do a full Heritage Impact Assessment.

V/O: The study has proved to be an invaluable resource, and they have also managed to declare the Elandsfontein dune field a Provincial Heritage Site.

Mary: The Elansdfontein mining site really has the potential to be a very important site.

V/O: Heritage Western Cape Board member Mary Leslie is cautiously optimistic about this collaboration.

Mary: It could be positive for us; it could expose ancient paleontological layers of bones that we would not have probably access to otherwise. It could also be disastrous if something goes wrong with the monitoring and it isn’t able to proceed in the best possible way.

Michelle: Currently on site we have fulltime paleontologists and archeologists, and they have been involved in development and all the work that is done here. They have trained up the excavator drivers so if there are any finds we with it in an appropriate manner.

Wynand: The total project is a R1.3 billion project all in all. This plant is about R 850 million, R847 million as it stands here.

V/O: The holding company and major funder of the Elandsfontein Mine is Kropz Fertilizers.

Michelle: There is Kropz SA which is held by Kropz International, and that is registered in Luxembourg. So Kropz holds 70% of Elandsfontein and the balance of Elandsfontein is held by some empowerment partners.

V/O: While there has been robust opposition to the mine, there are many who welcome this massive economic investment to the area. The construction phase has provided over a thousand jobs, which is which is why the local municipality supported the project, says Andre Kruger.

Andre: What is going to happen should we have a mine in our vicinity? Automatically economic growth is a great positive point, because economic growth gives you immediately jobs.

Claire: There’s a scarcity of water in the Saldanha municipality. Where will the water come from that the mine is using?

V/O: They require between 2.5 and 3.5 million litres per day. We will be able to supply them with that water without any problem.

Claire: So it will have no effect on the residents?
Andre: No effect on the residents.

V/O: Elandsfontein is still waiting for an Air Emissions License and a Water Use License before they can start mining.

Claire: We did ask the Department of Water Affairs on whether they will grant the Water Use License, but they haven’t come back to us.

V/O: The mine will produce 1.3 million tons of phosphate per year, which will be shipped out of the port at Saldanha Bay. While some will be used to produce fertilizer locally, the bulk will be exported to India, Australia and New Zealand.

Carika: I’m hoping that that will get stopped, that there will be at least some example where people know they cant just come in and plunder our land and take out what they want, and leave us with a broken ecosystem, and no water and polluted water.
